units.t: Mythology. Episode three.
In this episode: King Arthur: how a legend was built, Māui and the myths of Polynesia and The Dreaming: law, land and story.
Part one. King Arthur: how a legend was built.
There may never have been a King Arthur.
Yet over a thousand years, writers in Wales, England and France assembled Camelot, the Round Table and the Holy Grail piece by piece.
Faint traces after Rome.
Roman authority in Britain collapsed in the early fifth century.
Over the next two hundred years, Anglo-Saxon groups settled much of what became England, while Britons held out in the west and north.
Written records are extremely thin, which is why legends could flourish.
A British monk, Gildas, writing in the sixth century, described a British victory over the Saxons at Mount Badon.
Tellingly, he never mentions Arthur.
The earliest possible reference is in a Welsh poem, Y Gododdin, which praises a warrior as brave, "though he was no Arthur".
Its date is uncertain and the line may be a later addition.
From these faint traces, a towering figure would grow.
Twelve battles.
Around 830, the Latin Historia Brittonum, traditionally linked to a monk named Nennius, listed twelve battles fought by Arthur, a "leader of battles", ending at Badon.
Some sites are impossible to locate, and one passage has him carrying an image of the Virgin Mary into combat.
A later Welsh chronicle, the Annales Cambriae, records Badon and also Camlann, "in which Arthur and Medraut fell".
Medraut would become the treacherous Mordred.
Early Welsh poems and tales show a different Arthur, leading heroes against giants, witches and a monstrous boar.
Most historians now think there is not enough evidence to say whether a real Arthur existed, though the debate continues.
Geoffrey's bestseller.
The Arthur most people know was launched by Geoffrey of Monmouth, a cleric in Oxford.
His History of the Kings of Britain, completed around 1136, claimed to be translated from an ancient British book, a claim most scholars doubt.
Geoffrey gave Arthur a dramatic life.
Merlin's magic lets Uther Pendragon visit Igerna at Tintagel, and Arthur is conceived.
As king, Arthur defeats the Saxons, conquers much of Europe and challenges Rome itself.
While he is away, his nephew Mordred seizes the throne and Guinevere.
Arthur returns, kills Mordred and is mortally wounded, then carried to the island of Avalon to be healed.
The book was a medieval sensation, surviving in more than two hundred manuscripts.
Knights, table and Grail.
Writers across the Channel dressed Geoffrey's warrior king in courtly fashion.
In 1155 the Norman poet Wace retold the history in French verse and introduced the Round Table, where no knight could claim the place of honour.
Later, Chrétien de Troyes shifted attention from Arthur to his knights.
He gave us the earliest surviving story of Lancelot's love for Guinevere, and first mentioned Camelot.
Chrétien's unfinished Perceval, from the 1180s, introduced a mysterious graal, a serving dish carried in a procession.
He died before explaining it.
Soon Robert de Boron identified the Grail as the vessel of the Last Supper, and later romances made the quest a spiritual test that most knights failed.
The pure Galahad, Lancelot's son, achieves it.
Malory and the returning king.
In 1191, monks at Glastonbury Abbey announced they had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere.
The abbey needed funds after a fire, and many historians suspect the find was staged.
It still tied Avalon to Glastonbury.
Nearly three centuries later, Sir Thomas Malory, who wrote at least part of his work in prison, gathered the French and English stories into one English prose narrative.
William Caxton printed it in 1485 as Le Morte d'Arthur, the main source for later retellings.
Legend said Arthur would return in Britain's hour of need, and he has.
Tennyson made him a model of Victorian duty.
T. H. White used him to think about power after two world wars.
Arthur stands for the hope of a just ruler, and the sadness when good kingdoms fall.
The key idea: Arthur's story grew from very thin records in the obscure centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.
Part two. Māui and the myths of Polynesia.
He fished up islands, slowed the sun and stole fire.
Māui, the trickster demigod, is a hero across thousands of kilometres of Pacific Ocean.
A hero of the Pacific.
Picture the vast triangle of Polynesia.
It runs from Aotearoa New Zealand in the south-west to Hawaiʻi in the north and Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, in the east.
Island peoples with shared ancestral roots tell stories of the same mischievous hero: Māui, a clever, cheeky, slightly reckless demigod whose adventures explain features of the world.
In a well-known telling, Māui was born early and his mother, Taranga, wrapped him in her topknot and cast him into the sea.
Seaweed and jellyfish protected him, and a sky ancestor raised him.
As a boy he returned to announce himself to his surprised family.
He begins as an outsider who must prove himself, as the youngest of several brothers.
Fishing up a land.
The most famous Māui story in Aotearoa tells how he hid in the bottom of his brothers' canoe when they went fishing.
Far out to sea, he revealed himself and lowered a magical hook made from the jawbone of his grandmother, Murirangawhenua.
He caught something enormous and hauled it up: a vast fish, which became the North Island.
Its Māori name, Te Ika a Māui, means the fish of Māui.
His brothers began hacking at the fish before it had settled, which is said to explain the North Island's mountains and valleys.
The South Island is often known as Te Waka a Māui, his canoe, and Stewart Island as Te Punga a Māui, its anchor stone.
Sun and fire.
The sun once raced across the sky so fast that people lacked daylight to fish, farm and cook.
Māui and his brothers plaited strong ropes, went to where the sun rose and snared it.
Māui beat it with his grandmother's jawbone until it agreed to travel more slowly.
In Hawaiian tradition, a similar feat happens on Haleakalā, 'house of the sun', on Maui.
In another story, Māui put out the village fires and visited the fire goddess Mahuika, who kept fire in her fingernails.
He tricked her into giving up nail after nail until one was left.
She threw it at him, setting the land ablaze.
Māui called on rain, and the last sparks escaped into certain trees, such as the kaikōmako.
That is why rubbing sticks of those woods together makes fire.
The death of a trickster.
Māui's final adventure is his most daring.
He wanted to defeat death itself, so that people could live forever.
Death was personified by Hine nui te pō, the great woman of the night, a guardian of the underworld.
Māui planned to crawl through her body while she slept, which would reverse the course of death.
He took birds with him and warned them to keep quiet.
But as he crawled, the sight was so comical that a little fantail, the pīwakawaka, burst into laughter.
Hine nui te pō woke and crushed Māui, and so all people remain mortal.
Like Gilgamesh, the hero fails to escape death, and the story asks listeners to accept mortality as part of life.
Stories still alive.
These stories are not museum pieces.
Many Māori trace their whakapapa, or genealogy, back through gods and ancestors, so myths and family history are deeply connected.
Māori creation traditions describe the sky father Ranginui and earth mother Papatūānuku, pushed apart by their son Tāne to let light into the world.
Matariki, the Māori new year marked by the rising of the Pleiades star cluster, became a New Zealand public holiday in 2022.
Māui reached a global audience in Disney's 2016 film Moana.
Many people enjoyed it, while some Pacific voices criticised the way Māui was portrayed and argued that sacred figures should be depicted with care.
That debate shows how much these stories still matter to the people who own them.
The key idea: Māui is a clever, underestimated demigod whose stories are told across Polynesia, from Aotearoa to Hawaiʻi.
Part three. The Dreaming: law, land and story.
For tens of thousands of years, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have carried knowledge in story, song and country.
'Dreamtime' barely begins to describe it.
More than Dreamtime.
Many Australians first meet Aboriginal spirituality through the word 'Dreamtime', imagined as a magical era long ago.
That misses a great deal.
The Dreaming links creation, law, kinship, land and daily responsibility.
It explains how the world came to be, and it tells people how to live and how to care for country.
Australia's First Peoples have lived here for at least 50,000 years.
There is no single version: each nation has its own beliefs and words.
Anthropologists popularised 'Dreamtime' in the late 1800s, translating an Arrernte word.
Many Aboriginal people find it clumsy, because it suggests something imaginary when these beliefs describe what is most real.
The Anangu speak of Tjukurpa, and the Warlpiri of Jukurrpa.
In the 1950s W. E. H. Stanner called it an 'everywhen': ancestral events continue to shape the present.
Ancestors and country.
In many Dreaming accounts, ancestral beings travelled across a formless or sleeping land, and their actions created its features.
A waterhole may mark where an ancestor rested, a ridge where one lay down, a rock formation where a battle took place.
These beings took many forms: animals, plants, people, stars, and powerful figures like the Rainbow Serpent.
Its stories appear in different ways across much of the continent and are often tied to water and fertility.
Because ancestors are believed to remain present in the land, country is not just scenery or property.
It is family, history and law all at once.
Many Aboriginal people speak of belonging to country, rather than country belonging to them.
Songlines across country.
The journeys of ancestral beings are often remembered as songlines, sometimes called Dreaming tracks.
A songline can stretch hundreds or even thousands of kilometres, crossing the lands of many nations.
Each group holds responsibility for its own section of the song.
Singing the verses in order works like a map.
It names waterholes, landmarks and food sources in sequence, which could help people travel safely through dry country.
Songlines also carry law, kinship rules and seasonal knowledge, and some follow patterns in the stars.
Researchers studying memory are keenly interested in how songs, places and stories together can hold huge amounts of information without writing.
For the custodians, though, songlines are first and foremost sacred.
Not every story is shared.
A key point for outsiders is that Dreaming knowledge is not public property.
Some stories are open, often told to children and visitors.
Others are restricted to people who have gone through certain ceremonies, or are known as men's business or women's business and kept within those groups.
Certain sites are sacred and should not be photographed or entered.
Rights to tell a story, paint its designs or sing its songs belong to particular custodians, who inherit that responsibility through kinship.
This is why respectful books, galleries and tourism operators work with traditional owners and seek permission.
It is also why this lesson does not retell specific sacred stories: the respectful way to hear them is from the people who hold them.
A living tradition.
At Uluru, Tjukurpa is present for the Anangu traditional owners, and the climbing route has deep spiritual significance.
For decades signs asked tourists not to climb, and many did anyway.
After the park was handed back to Anangu ownership in 1985 and leased to the national parks agency, the joint management board voted to end the climb.
It closed permanently in October 2019.
Visitors now walk around the base instead.
Colonisation caused enormous harm, including dispossession, language loss and the removal of children.
Yet ceremony, song and story survive, and communities are reviving languages.
Since the 1970s, painters from Papunya in the Western Desert have shared permitted aspects of their Dreamings through acrylic art.
When you hear a Welcome to Country, you hear a very old relationship with land.
The key idea: The Dreaming is a living system of law, belief and knowledge, and 'Dreamtime' is only a clumsy English label for it.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why could Arthur legends flourish in the centuries after Rome?
Answer. Written records from the period are extremely thin.
Question two. What pattern do Māui's stories share?
Answer. An underestimated outsider proves himself.
Question three. Why do many Aboriginal people find 'Dreamtime' a clumsy translation?
Answer. It suggests something imaginary, not real.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
